title: Between Acceptance and Doubt: Understanding Climate Change Beliefs Across Central Europe and the Middle East
content: Despite recent extreme weather events such as heatwaves, wildfires and heavy rainfall, some people still doubt in the reality of the ongoing climate change and that it is linked to human activities. We examined cognitive (anthropocentric and ecocentric worldviews, holistic mindset, religiosity) and emotional (concern about global warming) predictors of climate change acceptance and scepticism, together with personal and distant risk perception, in four countries differently vulnerable to climate impacts: Belarus, Lithuania, Poland and the United Arab Emirates. Participants (N = 986; Mage = 23.22; 70% female; 66.6% students) completed the New Environmental Paradigm scale, the Holistic-Causality Scale, a Risk Perception Index (close and distant risk), a single item on concern, and a 10-item climate change perception scale (real vs. dubious). Hierarchical regressions showed that acceptance of climate change as real was predicted by concern, ecocentric worldview, distant risk perception and holistic mindset, but not by personal risk. Scepticism was predicted by anthropocentric worldview, religiosity and, unexpectedly, personal risk perception, suggesting that seeing global warming as personally threatening may lead some people to reject its reality. Across countries, only two patterns were consistent: ecocentrism predicted acceptance and anthropocentrism predicted scepticism. Other predictors varied by country
